questions.question: In an R1CS, what form does a single constraint take?
options: A · w + B · w + C · w = 0
A(w) * B(w) = C(w) for polynomials A,B,C
e(A, B) = e(C, g) for a pairing e
questions.explanation: R1CS constraints are rank-1 bilinear constraints: two linear combinations of the witness multiply to a third.

questions.question: What is the vanishing polynomial for the constraint domain {1, 2, ..., m}?
options: Z(x) = x^m - 1
Z(x) = x - m
questions.explanation: Z(x) is the lowest-degree nonzero polynomial that evaluates to 0 at each domain point 1..m.

questions.question: After converting R1CS to QAP polynomials A(x), B(x), and C(x), what polynomial does the protocol want to be divisible by Z(x)?
options: P(x) = A(x) * B(x) - C(x)
P(x) = A(x) + B(x) - C(x)
P(x) = A(x) * B(x) + C(x)
P(x) = A(x) / B(x) - C(x)
questions.explanation: The core QAP identity is A(x)B(x) − C(x) = H(x)Z(x), i.e. divisibility of A(x)B(x) − C(x) by Z(x).

questions.question: Why does “P(x) is divisible by Z(x)” capture “all m constraints are satisfied” (in the toy model)?
options: Because Z(k)=0 for k=1..m, so divisibility implies P(k)=0 for all constraints
Because Z(x) is random, so divisibility is unlikely by chance
Because any polynomial can be divided by any other with zero remainder
Because divisibility implies P(x) has degree 0
questions.explanation: If P(x)=H(x)Z(x), then at every root k of Z we have P(k)=0, matching the per-constraint checks.

questions.question: What does Lagrange interpolation do for the R1CS → QAP reduction?
options: Builds polynomials whose values at x=1..m match the per-constraint coefficients
Finds the witness values w that satisfy the circuit
Computes elliptic curve pairings efficiently
Turns a polynomial into a hash function
questions.explanation: Each R1CS column becomes a polynomial by interpolating its m values over the constraint indices.

questions.question: Why does the witness vector include a fixed first entry equal to 1?
options: To encode constants inside linear combinations (e.g., “+5” or “=35”)
To make polynomial multiplication commutative
To prevent interpolation from failing
To make the proof zero-knowledge by itself
questions.explanation: The constant wire lets constraints express constants without adding new variables for each literal constant.

questions.question: Attack: if a verifier only checks A(s)B(s) − C(s) = H(s)Z(s) at one point s, how can a malicious prover forge a passing 'proof' without a valid witness?
options: Pick A(s), B(s), H(s) arbitrarily and set C(s) = A(s)B(s) − H(s)Z(s)
Pick s = 0 so that all polynomials become 0
Send the full witness w to the verifier
Increase the degree of Z(x) so the check is stronger
questions.explanation: One equation in several unknowns is underdetermined; without consistency-binding, the prover can choose values that satisfy the check at s.

questions.question: What extra ingredient does Pinocchio-style SNARK design add to stop the forging attack above?
options: Consistency checks that bind A(s), B(s), C(s) to the same witness coefficients (via commitments/pairings/KoE-style arguments)
A larger prime field p so forging is impossible
A faster polynomial multiplication algorithm
Replacing Z(x) with x^m − 1
questions.explanation: Pinocchio must ensure the prover can’t just pick evaluations; the proof must certify the values arise from the circuit polynomials and one witness.
